subject: ss-paediatric-surgery
title: Paediatric Surgery
curriculum: NMC Competency-Based MCh Paediatric Surgery Curriculum / NBEMS NEET-SS Surgical Group (Paediatric Surgery)
examPattern: NEET-SS Surgical Group paper (150 MCQs, 40 percent feeder MS General Surgery and 60 percent super-speciality). Within the super-speciality share, paediatric surgery is tested through neonatal surgical emergencies (atresias, malrotation with volvulus, NEC, abdominal wall defects), Hirschsprung disease and anorectal malformations, paediatric hernias and undescended testis, Wilms tumour and neuroblastoma, and paediatric trauma. Weight follows MCh Paediatric Surgery university papers (neonatal surgery, paediatric urology, paediatric surgical oncology, trauma), the INI-SS important-topic list and the exam-pyq overlays.
book: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd Edition 2025 (Elsevier) Chapter 117 (paediatric surgery) and Chapter 42 (paediatric trauma); Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Part XXII urologic chapters (paediatric urology: VUR, obstruction, bladder exstrophy, hypospadias); society guidelines (APSA, AUA, SIOP, NWTSG, COG, SIOPEL) for operative topics

sections.name: Neonatal physiology, fluids, nutrition and head-neck lesions

modules.name: Neonatal cardiopulmonary transition and thermal care

mustKnow.fact: Newborns lose heat through a large surface area with little subcutaneous fat and high insensible loss, and respond by nonshivering thermogenesis that raises oxygen use, so a thermoregulated isolette holds core temperature between 36 and 37.5 degrees in a neutral thermal environment.

Fetal blood bypasses the lungs through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, and after the first breath the foramen ovale closes while falling pulmonary vascular resistance raises pulmonary flow and the ductus closes with higher oxygen.

Hypoxemia and acidosis raise pulmonary vascular resistance and cause persistent pulmonary hypertension with right to left shunt, treated with inhaled nitric oxide which relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
Indomethacin closes a patent ductus arteriosus in premature infants, and a ductus that stays open is closed by catheter coil or by open surgical ligation.
The neonatal heart raises output by rate rather than stroke volume, so heart rate change and capillary refill are the sensitive markers of volume status and tissue perfusion.
The neonatal trachea is only 2.5 to 4 mm wide and plugs easily, and the healthy newborn breathes 40 to 60 times per minute with a tidal volume of 6 to 10 mL per kg.
Infants are obligate nasal and diaphragmatic breathers, so a blocked nose or a splinted diaphragm rapidly causes distress with flaring, grunting, retractions and cyanosis.

Surfactant raises functional residual capacity, the lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid marks lung maturity, and exogenous surfactant improves premature survival while bronchopulmonary dysplasia means oxygen need plus radiologic change beyond 28 days of life.

Insensible water loss follows gestation, 45 to 60 mL per kg per day in prematures under 1500 g and 30 to 35 mL per kg per day at term, rising further with radiant warmers, phototherapy and respiratory distress.

Physiologic water loss reaches 10 percent of body weight in the first 3 to 5 days of life, and maintenance reaches 100 to 130 mL per kg per day by the fourth day, with much higher needs in gastroschisis and necrotising enterocolitis.
The ideal minimum urine output in a newborn is 1 to 2 mL per kg per hour, and infants concentrate urine only to about 700 mOsm per kg in prerenal azotemia.

Daily sodium need is 2 to 4 mEq per kg and potassium need is 1 to 2 mEq per kg, usually given as 5 percent dextrose in 0.45 percent saline with 20 mEq per L of potassium at the calculated maintenance rate.

Gastric losses are replaced volume for volume with 0.45 percent saline with 20 mEq per L of potassium, while diarrhoeal, pancreatic and biliary losses are replaced with isotonic lactated Ringer solution.
Hypovolemia from acute hemorrhage is corrected with prompt blood products at a bolus of 10 to 20 mL per kg of packed red cells, plasma or 5 percent albumin.
Sepsis workup in neonates covers blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures, and subtle triggers include feed intolerance, temperature instability, poor refill, tachypnea and irritability.
Empiric neonatal antibiotics target group B streptococcus, methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, and invasive lines and tubes raise hospital acquired infection risk.
Weight gain is the most reliable marker of adequate calories, the enteral target is 120 calories per kg per day, and standard formula and breast milk carry 20 calories per ounce.
Half the energy in term infants under 2 weeks and 60 percent in prematures under 1200 g goes to growth, and continuous feeds suit a stressed gut before transition to bolus feeds.
Small liver and muscle glycogen stores make neonates prone to hypoglycemia with seizure risk, and the minimum glucose infusion rate is 4 to 6 mg per kg per minute.
Parenteral glucose rises by 1 to 2 mg per kg per minute daily to a maximum of 10 to 12 mg per kg per minute, and hyperglycemia may signal sepsis and must be investigated.

Protein need is 2 to 3.5 g per kg per day in infants, halves by 12 years and reaches the adult 1 g per kg per day by 18 years, and parenteral protein starts at 0.5 and rises by 0.5 daily to about 3.5 g per kg per day.

Nonprotein to protein calorie ratio stays at or above 150 to 1, and lipid infusions start at 0.5 and rise to 2.5 to 3.5 g per kg per day to prevent essential fatty acid deficiency with its dry scaly rash.
Lipids are given cautiously with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia because fatty acids displace bilirubin from albumin and free bilirubin crosses into brain causing kernicterus and mental retardation.

Prolonged parenteral nutrition causes cholestasis with bile acids rising first then direct bilirubin then liver enzymes, best treated by restoring enteral feeds, with omega 3 emulsion protective and fat soluble vitamins supplemented on total enteral feeds.

modules.name: Thyroglossal duct cyst and midline neck lesions

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Head and neck lesions)

mustKnow.fact: An upper midline cystic neck lesion in a toddler is a thyroglossal duct cyst until proved otherwise, arising at the foramen cecum and usually presenting at or just below the hyoid bone.
The thyroid descends from the foramen cecum attached by the thyroglossal duct, and failure of caudal migration leaves a lingual thyroid with no other thyroid tissue in the neck.
Ultrasound or radionuclide imaging identifies ectopic thyroid tissue before any midline neck surgery so the only functioning thyroid is never removed.
The Sistrunk procedure is the standard operation, removing the cyst with its tract, the central hyoid bone, and the tract above the hyoid to the tongue base.
Incomplete resection leaves recurrence in 40 to 50 percent of cases, so the hyoid core and suprahyoid tract must be taken in continuity.
Dermoid cysts of the forehead, lateral eyebrow, anterior fontanelle or postauricular space contain skin appendages like hair, while epidermoid cysts hold only epidermis and keratin debris.
Pilomatrixoma is a firm nontender hair follicle nodule needing excision when painful or infected, and midline scalp lesions need ultrasound to exclude a communicating cephalocele.
Most scalp dermoids need only clinical diagnosis before excision, but lesions can enlarge over time and erode bone, so symptomatic nodules are removed.

modules.name: Branchial cleft remnants and lateral neck lesions

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Head and neck lesions)

mustKnow.fact: Branchial remnants present as lateral neck masses from failed regression of arches, clefts and pouches, appearing as cysts, sinuses, fistulas, cartilaginous rests, dermal pits or skin tags with mucoid drainage.
Second branchial cleft anomalies are the most common type, with the external opening along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid usually between its upper half and lower third.

The second cleft fistula rises along the carotid sheath to the hyoid, turns medially between the carotid bifurcation, and passes the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves behind the digastric to end in the tonsillar fossa.
Long tortuous fistulas need stepladder counterincisions for complete excision, because residual tract guarantees recurrence or injury to adjacent nerves and vessels.

First branchial anomalies sit in front of or behind the ear or upper neck near the mandible, with fistulas coursing through the parotid through or around facial nerve branches to the external auditory canal.
Third branchial remnants sit at the suprasternal notch or clavicle, can descend into the mediastinum, present as firm cysts or abscesses in toddlers, and often contain cartilage.

Fixed nontender enlarging supraclavicular nodes with night sweats and weight loss raise malignancy concern and need chest imaging for mediastinal nodes, while acute bilateral viral nodes need observation alone.

Staphylococcus aureus and group A streptococcus cause most acute pyogenic lymphadenitis, while fluctuant violaceous nodes suggest nontuberculous mycobacteria needing excision because they resist chemotherapy.

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Head and neck lesions)

mustKnow.fact: Cystic hygroma is an endothelial lined multiloculated lymphatic malformation of the jugular sacs, usually posterior neck, with about 50 percent present at birth and other sites being axilla, mediastinum, groin and retroperitoneum.

A large fetal neck mass threatens the airway at birth, and prenatal ultrasound with fetal magnetic resonance defines extent and mass effect so an ex utero intrapartum treatment procedure can secure the airway.

Cystic hygromas bleed and infect easily, magnetic resonance maps the lymphatic channels, and surgery demands complete excision with tedious ligation of branches because blunt or cautery dissection causes recurrence and infection.
When complete excision is unsafe, sclerotherapy with bleomycin, doxycycline or OK-432 from Streptococcus pyogenes is an effective nonsurgical option.
Cat-scratch disease is a self-limited painful regional adenopathy from Bartonella henselae, confirmed by lymph node polymerase chain reaction which beats immunofluorescence in specificity.
Nontuberculous mycobacterial nodes are fluctuant with violaceous skin, diagnosed by positive acid fast cultures with tuberculin skin testing, and need surgical excision for cure.
Ultrasound detects nodes with central necrosis needing urgent surgery, and fixed supraclavicular nodes with constitutional symptoms need malignancy workup including chest radiography.

Viral bilateral cervical nodes from adenovirus, influenza or respiratory syncytial virus need observation only, while bacterial nodes need antibiotics with surgery reserved for necrosis or mycobacteria.

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Pediatric critical care: extracorporeal life support)

mustKnow.fact: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation gives temporary cardiopulmonary support with carbon dioxide removal, oxygenation and circulatory support for refractory respiratory or cardiac failure, sepsis and extracorporeal resuscitation.

Meconium aspiration is the most common neonatal indication with survival above 90 percent, alongside respiratory distress syndrome, persistent pulmonary hypertension, sepsis and congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

ECMO is indicated near 80 percent predicted mortality, with an alveolar arterial gradient above 610 for 8 to 12 hours or above 620 for 6 hours with barotrauma and hypotension, or an oxygen index above 40.
The oxygen index equals inspired oxygen fraction times mean airway pressure times 100 divided by arterial oxygen, and values above 40 predict 80 percent mortality without ECMO.

Contraindications are severe prematurity with intracranial bleed risk, weight under 2 kg, existing intracranial bleed, irreversible lung disease like alveolar dysplasia, cyanotic heart disease, lethal genetic defects and intractable coagulopathy.

Venoarterial cannulation uses the right internal jugular vein and common carotid artery in young children, the carotid is usually ligated at decannulation which babies tolerate, and older children use femoral vessels with a distal perfusion cannula for the leg.
Venovenous bypass uses a double lumen single cannula, works for respiratory failure with good cardiac function, and restores hemodynamic stability through well oxygenated blood.

Bleeding is the most common complication at cannula, thoracic and intracranial sites, and gestation under 34 weeks best predicts intracranial hemorrhage, with recovery shown by rising arterial oxygen, better compliance and clearing radiograph before clamp trial.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurs in about 1 in 2000 to 5000 births, with Bochdalek posterolateral defects making 70 to 75 percent, Morgagni anterior defects 23 to 28 percent, and central defects 2 to 7 percent.

Bochdalek hernias are left sided in 85 percent, right sided in 13 percent and bilateral in 2 percent, and both lungs suffer hypoplasia with thickened arteriolar muscle that drives pulmonary hypertension.
Prenatal ultrasound from 15 weeks shows mediastinal shift, juxtacardiac gastric dilatation and polyhydramnios, and an intrathoracic liver plus cardiac or chromosomal anomalies predicts poor outcome.
The lung to head ratio compares contralateral lung to head circumference against gestational norms and predicts early neonatal morbidity for counseling and delivery planning.

At birth the infant shows grunting, retractions and cyanosis with a scaphoid abdomen, diminished breath sounds, bowel sounds in the chest and shifted heart tones with pre and postductal saturation differences.

Fetal endoluminal tracheal occlusion places a tracheal balloon at 27 to 29 weeks with later retrieval to trap lung fluid and grow the lung, and the TOTAL trial showed survival benefit at discharge and 6 months.

Stable infants are repaired at 48 to 72 hours to avoid vascular lability, bleeding is worse on ECMO so some repair after weaning, and closure uses interrupted nonabsorbable sutures with Gore-Tex patch for large defects.

Reduction can lose abdominal domain and cause compartment syndrome needing a silo or skin only closure, and survivors face chronic lung disease, reflux, scoliosis, growth failure and developmental delay.

CPAM is the most common congenital lung lesion at 1 in 25000 to 35000 births, a multicystic hamartoma from pseudoglandular airway obstruction that communicates with the bronchial tree on pulmonary blood supply.
Many prenatal lesions regress in the third trimester, antenatal betamethasone shrinks lesions and reverses hydrops, and severe fetal compression with hydrops may need in utero intervention.
Symptomatic newborns show tachypnea, grunting and oxygen need, while older children present with recurrent pneumonia, pneumothorax, hemoptysis or lung abscess.
The Stocker system now has five types 0 to IV by airway origin, cyst content and radiology, replacing the old macrocystic, mixed and solid three type scheme with better prognostic value.
Resection is advised in every child without spontaneous regression within the first 2 years of life to prevent infection, allow compensatory lung growth and remove malignant risk.
Postnatal workup uses chest radiograph for cysts or pneumothorax plus computed tomography or magnetic resonance to separate CPAM from sequestration and diaphragmatic hernia.
Severe birth asphyxia from lung compression and mediastinal shift needs emergency resection or ECMO, since the compressed lung cannot ventilate.
CPAM shares prenatal ultrasound and fetal magnetic resonance detection with sequestration, and Doppler plus postnatal imaging defines the systemic versus pulmonary blood supply.

Sequestration is nonfunctional dysplastic lung under 6 percent of congenital lung anomalies, with no tracheobronchial connection and a systemic arterial supply from the thoracic or infradiaphragmatic aorta.

Intralobar sequestration sits inside normal visceral pleura with pulmonary venous drainage, makes two thirds of cases in the posterior basal lower lobe, and presents with recurrent pneumonia in one segment.

Extralobar sequestration has its own pleura with systemic venous drainage, hides between diaphragm and lower lobe or below the diaphragm, and associates with diaphragmatic hernia, pectus and enteric duplication cysts.

Extralobar lesions never form big cysts or spontaneous pneumothorax for lack of airway connection, but they can infarct, infect, bleed, twist, or shunt enough blood to cause high output cardiac failure in neonates.
More than two thirds of prenatal lesions regress as body growth outstrips blood supply, and fetuses are watched with serial ultrasound for effusion, polyhydramnios or hydrops.
Postnatal Doppler ultrasound defines cystic versus solid texture and maps the feeding systemic artery, while computed tomography or magnetic resonance is reserved for unclear or worrisome scans.
Air or air fluid inside an extralobar lesion is abnormal and suggests a fistula to the gut, since these lesions never communicate with the airway.
Surgery is segmentectomy or lobectomy for intralobar disease and mass resection for extralobar disease by open or thoracoscopic technique.

modules.name: Eventration, lobar emphysema and bronchogenic cyst

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Diaphragmatic and bronchopulmonary conditions)

mustKnow.fact: Eventration is an abnormally high hemidiaphragm from congenital weakness, birth trauma with upper plexus Erb palsy of C5 to C6 that can include the C3 to C5 phrenic nerve in extensive injuries, or acquired phrenic injury during cardiac surgery.
Fluoroscopy or ultrasound showing absent or paradoxical inspiratory movement confirms eventration and separates it from congenital diaphragmatic hernia on plain radiograph.
Repair is indicated for distress or ventilator dependence, done open or laparoscopically by plicating the diaphragm with multiple interrupted nonabsorbable sutures.
Congenital lobar emphysema affects 1 in 20000 to 30000 births with a 3 to 1 male excess in the first 6 months, from deficient bronchial cartilage causing expiratory collapse and air trapping.
The left upper lobe leads at 43 percent, then right middle lobe at 32 percent and right upper lobe at 21 percent, and the lucency must never be mistaken for a pneumothorax.
Positive pressure ventilation worsens auto positive end expiratory pressure in these infants, and progressive mediastinal shift with worsening symptoms needs prompt open lobectomy.

Bronchogenic cysts arise at 3 to 6 weeks of gestation in 1 in 42000 to 68000 births with male excess, sit near the carina and right hilum when early and peripheral when late, and appear as nonenhancing mucus filled spheres on computed tomography.

All bronchogenic cysts are resected even when silent because compression, infection and rare malignancy threaten, with parenchymal cysts usually communicating with a bronchus and mediastinal ones usually blind.
Atresia with or without fistula occurs in 1 in 1500 to 3000 births with mild male excess, a third are low birth weight, and 60 to 70 percent carry associated anomalies.

Faulty division of the foregut at 4 weeks causes the defects, 10 percent cluster as VATERL with vertebral, anorectal, tracheal, oesophageal, renal and radial anomalies, and the C type with proximal atresia and distal fistula dominates.

Drooling with choking on first feeds plus a tube that recoils at the thoracic inlet defines atresia, maternal polyhydramnios is prominent in pure atresia at 86 percent, and distal fistula distends the stomach with air.

Abdominal gas confirms a distal fistula while a gasless abdomen after failed tube passage means pure atresia, contrast swallow is banned for aspiration risk, and echo plus renal ultrasound screen heart and kidney defects.

Care is upright prone nursing with continuous sump suction, broad spectrum antibiotics, and no routine intubation since positive pressure drives air through the fistula, with distal tube advancement, fistula balloon, or emergent gastrostomy to water seal as rescue.

Right thoracotomy suits a left aortic arch while either side suits a right arch, repair is extrapleural with azygos division and immediate absorbable closure of the 1 to 2 mm fistula stump, and the upper pouch mobilises widely while the lower pouch is handled gently for its segmental blood supply.
The Spitz score predicts survival by weight and cardiac disease, with over 1500 g and no major cardiac lesion at 97 percent, either risk factor at 59 percent, and both at 22 percent.

Sequelae are reflux in 25 to 50 percent, stricture in 15 to 30 percent, leak in 10 to 20 percent and tracheomalacia in 8 to 15 percent, and thoracoscopy with preoperative bronchoscopy for tracheomalacia and second fistula is now standard.

modules.name: Long gap atresia and isolated fistula

mustKnow.fact: Pure atresia needs a gastrostomy for feeds since primary joining is impossible neonatally, secretions are managed by indwelling tube, and delayed primary anastomosis follows radiologic elongation usually at 4 to 6 months.
The divided distal end can be hitched to prevertebral fascia with a hemoclip so growth lengthens it for later joining, and abandoned esophagomyotomy is obsolete because it wrecks motility.
Cervical esophagostomy is reserved for unmanageable aspiration, and replacement with stomach, colon or small bowel conduit waits until 1 to 2 years of age.
The gap is judged by contrast through the gastrostomy against an indwelling radiopaque upper tube, choosing primary joining versus colonic interposition.
Isolated H type fistula presents late with feeding cough and choking, is fixed through a cervical incision near the thoracic inlet, and is mapped by rigid bronchoscopy with guidewire cannulation.
Recurrent fistula is mapped the same way with Fogarty catheter placement to guide safe redo dissection.
Mortality tracks cardiac and chromosomal anomalies rather than the atresia itself, so full anomaly screening precedes any repair plan.
A right sided aortic arch raises arch anomalies and postoperative complications, influences thoracotomy side choice, and is defined by preoperative chest film and echocardiography.

Transient vomiting from an immature lower sphincter usually resolves between 6 and 12 months, while persistent severe reflux causes failure to thrive, recurrent bronchitis, asthma like wheeze, apnea and even stridor events.
Acid burns can stricture the oesophagus and convert squamous lining to Barrett columnar metaplasia needing periodic surveillance for dysplasia.
Contrast studies show anatomy and mechanical causes like webs and malrotation but lack specificity, while endoscopy shows mucosal injury and detects eosinophilic oesophagitis that mimics reflux.
The 24 hour oesophageal pH study is the gold standard, counting acid episodes with total and longest durations, and combined impedance pH adds liquid versus gas detection.
Radionuclide gastric emptying clears about 50 percent of the meal by 60 minutes and 80 percent by 90 minutes, while manometry is rarely used in children.
First therapy is thickened feeds, smaller volumes and positioning plus acid suppression, and surgery is reserved for life threatening events, failure to thrive or stricture.

Nissen 360 degree wrap is the gold standard but risks bloating and dysphagia despite limited hiatal dissection, while Toupet 270 and Thal 180 degree partial wraps trade some efficacy for fewer side effects.
Laparoscopy is the standard route, poor motility predicts dysphagia after a full wrap, and prophylactic wraps in neurologically impaired children stay controversial for weak airway protection.

sections.name: Pylorus, intestinal atresias, volvulus and necrotising enterocolitis

mustKnow.fact: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis affects 1 in 300 to 900 live births, peaks at 2 to 8 weeks, hits males four times more often, and first born males carry the highest risk.

Circular muscle hypertrophy obstructs the gastric outlet, absent nitric oxide synthase in pyloric tissue is implicated, and infants develop progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting yet still crave feeds.
A palpable epigastric olive by an experienced examiner is pathognomonic and needs no imaging, with visible left to right gastric peristalsis as a supporting sign.
Ultrasound diagnosis needs pyloric muscle over 3 to 4 mm thick or over 15 to 18 mm long with functional outlet obstruction, and equivocal cases may use contrast study with aspiration caution.
Vomited hydrochloric acid causes hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with dehydration, and anesthesia before correction risks postoperative apnea from lost carbon dioxide drive.

Resuscitation starts with a 20 mL per kg saline bolus, then D5 half saline with 20 mEq per L potassium at 1.5 times maintenance after urine flows, aiming for bicarbonate under 30 and chloride above 95 mEq per L.

Ramstedt Fredet pyloromyotomy splits the hypertrophied muscle to bulging mucosa with independent wall motion and no mucosal injury, done open or laparoscopically with laparoscopy giving shorter stay and fewer wound infections.

Postoperative vomiting is common and self limited, full thickness perforation is under 1 percent and commoner with laparoscopy, and emesis beyond 7 to 14 days needs contrast study for incomplete myotomy.

Duodenal atresia comes from failed recanalization of the solid cord stage, spanning stenosis, windsock web, fibrous cord and complete gap, and associates with prematurity, Down syndrome, malrotation, preduodenal portal vein, annular pancreas and biliary atresia.
Obstruction lies distal to the ampulla in 85 percent so infants vomit bile, prenatal ultrasound detects it, and plain film shows the double bubble before tube decompression removes gastric air.
Distal air on film mandates contrast study to exclude malrotation with midgut volvulus, a true surgical emergency that outranks the atresia itself.
Repair is diamond shaped duodenoduodenostomy, increasingly laparoscopic, with tapering duodenoplasty for a hugely dilated proximal duodenum and transduodenal web excision sparing the ampulla.

Jejunoileal atresia is the most common gut atresia at 1 in 2000 births from intrauterine vascular accident, presenting with bilious vomiting, distention and no meconium, with 10 to 15 percent multiple atresias needing intraoperative saline testing of the distal bowel.

The five types run from web to fibrous cord to V gap to apple peel IIIb with retrograde ileocolic supply risking anastomotic failure and short gut, to string of sausages type IV, and cystic fibrosis affects 10 percent.
Surgery preserves maximal length with tapering enteroplasty for dilated proximal bowel, resection only with adequate length, and survival exceeds 90 percent.

Colonic atresia is rarest at 5 to 10 percent of atresias and 1 in 20000 births, shows featureless dilated loops without haustra, and is confirmed by contrast enema with repair by diverting end colostomy or primary anastomosis.
Autopsy rotational anomalies reach 2 to 5 per 1000 births but clinical disease is 1 in 6000, 90 percent present before 12 months, and up to 1 percent first present as adults.

Failed fixation leaves duodenojejunal and ileocecal junctions close together on a narrow superior mesenteric stalk that twists, and associated defects include diaphragmatic hernia, gastroschisis and omphalocele.

Acute bilious vomiting in a lethargic newborn is ominous for volvulus, while intermittent crampy pain with malabsorption and melena marks partial twists, and a distended abdomen with acidosis signals life threatening ischemia.

Upper gastrointestinal contrast is the study of choice in stable patients, showing a bird beak in the third duodenum or a corkscrew tapering, with reversed superior mesenteric vein and artery on ultrasound as support.
An acutely ill child with suspected volvulus goes straight to theatre with resuscitation en route, because every minute of ischemia costs bowel length.

The 1936 Ladd procedure untwists the mesentery, divides Ladd bands from right colon to side wall, straightens the duodenum, opens the mesenteric base across the vein, removes the appendix, and lays the bowel broad and flat with cecum in the left upper quadrant.

Suturing cecum or duodenum to the wall has no proven benefit, borderline bowel gets a 24 to 36 hour second look, recurrence reaches 10 percent, and volvulus causes about 18 percent of paediatric short gut.
An orogastric tube passed beyond the pylorus after Ladd repair excludes a coexisting duodenal web, since dual pathology is described.

Necrotising enterocolitis is the most common gastrointestinal surgical emergency in neonates, driven by ischemia, bacterial overgrowth, cytokines and feeds, with prematurity as the dominant risk and breast milk based gradual feeds lowering incidence.

Hallmarks are distention, tenderness, cellulitis, bloody stools and feed intolerance with temperature instability, apnea and bradycardia, and 80 percent strike in the first month with feeds in the first days.
Pneumatosis intestinalis from bacterial hydrogen is pathognomonic, with portal venous gas, fixed loops, ascites and free air as companions, usually hitting distal ileum and ascending colon.
Over half the cases resolve medically with tube decompression, fluids and broad spectrum antibiotics under close watch for surgical triggers.
Free air is the absolute operative indication, while deterioration, acidosis, cellulitis, a palpable mass, fixed loop and portal gas are relative indications for exploration.

Principles are resecting dead bowel, saving length, and diverting with a stoma or damage control discontinuity, with second look at 24 to 48 hours for merely ischemic segments and primary anastomosis only for rare focal perforations.
Bedside peritoneal drainage matches laparotomy for survival, parenteral need and stay in infants under 1500 g in a multicentre randomised trial, and sometimes proves definitive.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117; Moss et al NEJM 2006

mustKnow.fact: Strictures complicate 10 percent after any management, typically at the splenic flexure, so contrast enema precedes stoma reversal, while surgically managed disease carries 10 to 50 percent mortality plus neurodevelopmental delay.

Short bowel means inadequate absorption for growth from massive resection or dysfunction, led by necrotising enterocolitis at 35 percent, atresia at 25 percent, gastroschisis at 18 percent and midgut volvulus at 14 percent.

Function depends on villous architecture, length, diameter, ileocecal valve, residual segments, stasis and bacterial overgrowth, with 35 to 40 cm giving a 50 percent chance of parenteral weaning plus 4 percent per extra centimeter.
Jejunum absorbs most macronutrients and minerals while ileum handles carbohydrates, proteins, fluids, electrolytes, bile acids, vitamin B12 and fat soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
The terminal ileum adapts best so the valve likely just marks its presence, and the colon importantly reclaims water and electrolytes after massive resection.

Adaptation is aided by elemental diet, growth factors and titrated parenteral support, while old transit slowing tricks like reversed segments, recirculating loops, valves, colon interposition and pacing failed and were abandoned.

The Bianchi procedure splits dilated bowel longitudinally on two mesenteric leaves and joins ends in series, halving diameter and doubling length, but risks vascular injury and is technically demanding.

Serial transverse enteroplasty staples dilated bowel transversely in alternating V shapes to narrow and lengthen, is easier and repeatable, and a 36 patient review showed 53 percent length gain with 42 percent reaching autonomy.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117; Kim et al 2003

mustKnow.fact: Multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation governs selection and follow up, since surgery alone never replaces careful nutritional and medical management.

Meconium ileus is the earliest cystic fibrosis manifestation in 10 to 15 percent of patients, from CFTR chloride failure making 80 to 90 percent protein secretions, with disease in 1 in 1000 to 2000 births.

The triad in the first 24 to 48 hours is generalized distention, bilious vomiting and no meconium, with polyhydramnios in 20 percent and soap bubble ground glass loops without air fluid levels on film.

Water soluble Gastrografin enema shows a small caliber colon with terminal pellets and relieves obstruction in 75 percent by drawing water in, with perforation under 3 percent under close hydration watch.
Pilocarpine sweat chloride above 60 mEq per L definitively confirms cystic fibrosis, with CFTR gene testing as the faster alternative.

Failed enema or 5 mL of 10 percent N-acetylcysteine every 6 hours by tube leads to surgery, where enterotomy with warm saline or 4 percent acetylcysteine washout and mucosal sparing evacuation beats routine resection.

Complicated disease with in utero perforation gives calcification, pseudocyst, adhesive peritonitis or ascites on film, while distal ileal obstruction syndrome in older patients from missed enzymes or dehydration usually responds to enemas or oral polyethylene glycol.
High strength pancreatic enzyme replacement treats exocrine failure but can cause fibrosing colonopathy needing stricture resection.

Meconium plug syndrome is usually not cystic fibrosis but signals Hirschsprung disease, maternal diabetes or hypothyroidism, shows a microcolon packed with plugs to the dilated proximal colon, and is both diagnosed and cured by contrast enema without surgery.

Hirschsprung disease is distal aganglionosis of myenteric and submucosal plexuses in 1 in 5000 births with fourfold male excess, 3 to 5 percent with Down syndrome, and RET oncogene locus on chromosome 10 in familial cases.
Failed relaxation of the distal colon and internal sphincter creates functional obstruction where the narrow distal segment is abnormal and the dilated proximal bowel is normal.
Aganglionosis starts at the anorectal line with transition to normal colon in rectosigmoid in 80 percent, splenic or transverse colon in 17 percent, and total colon with small bowel in 8 percent.

Over 90 percent present as newborns with distention and bilious vomiting plus no meconium in 24 hours, while missed cases return with chronic constipation, and enterocolitis with diarrhea, fever, hematochezia, shock and death is the leading killer.

Contrast enema shows a narrow distal rectum with transition zone and dilated proximal sigmoid, and contrast retained at 24 hours strongly indicates disease while also excluding plug, small left colon and atresia.

Suction rectal biopsy proximal to the dentate line is the gold standard, needing specimens 5 mm to 1 cm above it and two samples 1 cm apart posteriorly in infants, with absent ganglia, hypertrophied trunks, acetylcholinesterase staining and calretinin as criteria.

Swenson full thickness dissection, Soave endorectal dissection with posterior cuff myotomy usually laparoscopic assisted and transanal, and Duhamel retrorectal pull with side to side neorectum give similar function after frozen section confirmed ganglionated pull through.

Most undergo one stage pull through after irrigations with a soft red rubber catheter and saline to clear effluent, leveling colostomy reserved for failed irrigation or long segment disease, and follow up controls constipation and soiling with rebiopsy for transition zone at the anastomosis.
Imperforate anus occurs in 1 in 5000 births with 58 percent male, spanning perineal groove to cloaca, with rectobulbar urethral fistula commonest in males and rectovestibular commonest in females.
The urorectal septum divides the cloaca by week 6 and the anal membrane resorbs, so septum failure gives bowel to urinary fistulas and membrane failure gives stenosis or anterior perineal openings.

A cloaca fuses rectum, vagina and urethra into one channel with 3 cm marking short versus long defects, a single female orifice means cloaca, and two orifices suggest urogenital sinus with normal anus.
Sacral and spinal defects affect a third of patients, absent two or more vertebrae predicts poor bowel and bladder continence, and tethered cord, lipomeningocele and fatty filum need imaging.

Genitourinary anomalies rise with defect height to 90 percent in cloaca and rectovesical fistula but only 10 percent in perineal fistula, with reflux and hydronephrosis commonest, so renal ultrasound and voiding cystourethrogram are routine plus echo and orogastric tube for cardiac and oesophageal associations.

Perineal and vestibular fistulas undergo single stage repair without stoma, blind pouches and rectourinary fistulas need a divided sigmoid colostomy with mucous fistula first, then posterior sagittal anorectoplasty at 3 to 6 months with electrical sphincter mapping, then stoma closure.
Anal dilatations start 2 weeks after anorectoplasty and continue months past closure, and anorectal manometry style serial dilation alone suffices for a normally placed stenotic anus.

Social continence is the goal with 75 percent achieving voluntary bowel movements though half of those still soil, and constipation remains the commonest sequela needing a bowel management program of softeners and laxatives.

Ileocolic telescoping peaks from 3 months to 3 years with half under 1 year and under a quarter after age 2, usually idiopathic at the lymphoid rich ileocecal valve after viral illness or rotavirus vaccine.

Colicky pain with leg drawing and quiet intervals plus vomiting, currant jelly stools and a palpable mass define it, and lead points reach 12 percent in older children with Meckel diverticulum commonest alongside polyps, Henoch Schonlein bleeding and duplications.

Ultrasound target sign in transverse view and pseudokidney sign longitudinally trigger air or contrast enema, while plain film mass, sparse colonic gas or complete obstruction supports the diagnosis in half the cases.

Enema reduction succeeds above 80 percent with reflux into terminal ileum and mass resolution, many children discharge without admission, repeat enema hours later salvages some failures, and recurrence is 11 percent usually within 24 hours.

Peritonitis, instability, purely small bowel location and third recurrence need surgery, reduction pushes proximally in retrograde fashion, resection is rare, and post reduction fever resolves spontaneously.

Meckel diverticulum is the commonest gut anomaly at 2 percent, a true diverticulum from failed vitelline regression at 5 to 7 weeks, with heterotopic gastric mucosa in over 70 percent and pancreatic tissue in 5 percent.
The rule of twos places it 2 feet from the valve at 2 inches long symptomatic by 2 years, and technetium pertechnetate scanning detects gastric but never pancreatic mucosa.

Bleeding is painless and massive under 5 years from the mesenteric sided ulcer opposite the diverticulum mouth, so segmental resection is gold standard while quiet V diverticulectomy with transverse closure suits nonbleeders, and incidental quiet diverticula are left alone.
Diagnosis now rests on blood tests plus ultrasound or computed tomography rather than history and examination alone, with magnetic resonance added at some centres to cut radiation.
Clinical pathways standardise antibiotics, technique and near zero outpatient opioids, and laparoscopic appendectomy is the standard operation.
Simple appendicitis gets preoperative piperacillin tazobactam monotherapy and safe operation within 24 hours without added perforation risk.
Complicated disease continues antibiotics after surgery or uses percutaneous drainage with or without delayed interval appendectomy.
Up to 40 percent of perforated cases develop postoperative abscess needing drainage or continued antibiotics.
A multi institutional trial found nonoperative care acceptable for carefully selected uncomplicated cases, though long term efficacy needs more study.
Nonoperative care proved useful during COVID-19 in children whose concurrent respiratory infection made anesthesia hazardous.
Contained abscess in complicated appendicitis is drained percutaneously first, with delayed interval appendectomy weeks later once inflammation settles.

Biliary atresia obliterates intra and extrahepatic ducts in 1 in 5000 to 12000 infants by immune injury, viral trigger or HLA and CFC1 predisposition, with splenic, venous and intestinal malrotation associations.
Type III at the porta hepatis exceeds 90 percent while types I and II keep patent common or hepatic ducts and may allow direct biliary intestinal anastomosis.

Jaundice with pale stools and dark urine from birth progressing to failure to thrive and ascites demands liver workup if still jaundiced after 14 days at term, with direct bilirubin above 2.0 mg per dL marking liver disease.

Workup excludes TORCH, hepatitis B and C, alpha 1 antitrypsin, cystic fibrosis, galactosemia, tyrosinemia and endocrine causes, while ultrasound shows absent or atrophic gallbladder and HIDA shows uptake without duodenal emptying.
Intraoperative cholangiography with no duodenal contrast confirms disease and triggers Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy dissecting the fibrous plate to liver capsule with Roux en Y drainage.
Operation before 60 days gives 60 percent two year native liver survival versus 40 percent after 90 days, so timing decides outcome.

The START randomised trial showed no drainage benefit from high dose post Kasai steroids with earlier serious adverse events and impaired growth, though pulse steroids still treat cholangitis, and 45 to 60 percent develop ascending cholangitis on antibiotics.

Kasai never cures and over 70 percent progress to cirrhosis, yet 80 percent of drained infants reach 10 years before transplant, and transplant gives 86 percent patient and 73 percent graft survival at 10 years.
Choledochal cysts dilate the bile duct in 1 in 100000 to 150000 births with 3 to 4 fold female excess and links to duodenal and colonic atresia, imperforate anus and pancreas divisum.

Todani types are I in 50 to 80 percent, II diverticulum in 2 percent, III choledochocele in 1.4 to 4.5 percent, IV intra plus extrahepatic in 15 to 35 percent, and V Caroli intrahepatic only in 20 percent.
Pancreaticobiliary malunion with a common channel over 6 mm lets activated enzymes reflux and inflame the duct wall with high bile amylase, offering the leading pathogenesis.

The full triad of jaundice, right upper quadrant mass and pain occurs in under 20 percent though 85 percent show at least two, infants present with obstructive jaundice and a mass while older children have intermittent pain, fever and jaundice.

Ultrasound shows a cyst separate from gallbladder, HIDA shows absent then delayed uptake with duodenal emptying, magnetic resonance maps the whole tree and pancreas, and endoscopic retrograde study is rarely needed.
Prompt complete excision with Roux en Y hepaticojejunostomy is mandatory because retained cyst carries up to 6 percent malignancy, and unsafe dissection is enucleated rather than left behind.
Separating biliary and pancreatic drainage arrests the inflammatory drive under the malunion theory, and surveillance ultrasound watches for anastomotic stricture.
Rupture causes bile peritonitis and chronic inflammation brings stones, cholangitis and strictures, so complications of delay reinforce early excision.

sections.name: Abdominal wall, chest wall and pancreaticobiliary

mustKnow.fact: Midgut herniates through the umbilical ring and returns with rotation and closure by week 11, and failure leaves an omphalocele centrally or gastroschisis on the right.
Omphalocele is a central defect over 4 cm with an intact sac of outer amnion and inner peritoneum, while defects under 4 cm are called umbilical cord hernias.

About half carry anomalies including Beckwith Wiedemann gigantism with macroglossia and umbilical defect, trisomies 13, 15, 18 and 21, bladder or cloacal exstrophy, and Cantrell pentalogy of omphalocele, anterior diaphragmatic hernia, sternal cleft, ectopia cordis and ventricular septal defect.
Sac preservation and hypothermia prevention come first with full anomaly workup, then primary closure for small to medium defects.
Large defects close with prosthetic patch, porcine submucosal biomaterial, skin flap, or silo with staged reduction and closure.
Giant omphaloceles are painted with povidone iodine or silver nitrate escharotics so the sac thickens and epithelialises for delayed closure.
Survival follows lung maturity and anomaly severity rather than defect size alone.
Umbilical cord hernias under 4 cm behave like small omphaloceles and usually allow primary fascial closure without patch.
Gastroschisis always lies right of an intact cord at the obliterated right umbilical vein, has no sac, and exposes bowel to amniotic fluid causing thickening, edema and inflammation.
The fascial defect is typically 4 cm, intestinal atresia complicates up to 15 percent, but other major anomalies are rare unlike omphalocele.
After birth the infant goes into a warm saline filled bowel bag to the nipple line to limit heat and fluid loss while allowing inspection and detection of twisting.
Primary reduction succeeds in 50 to 80 percent without excess tension, failures get a ringed silo with gradual bedside reduction over days then fascial and skin closure.
Safe intraabdominal pressure stays under 15 mm Hg to avoid compartment syndrome, and sutureless closure covers reduced bowel and cord with a watertight clear dressing changed at 4 days.
With coexisting atresia the wall closes first and bowel repair waits 6 to 8 weeks because inflamed bowel forbids immediate anastomosis.

Late necrotising enterocolitis follows repair in up to 20 percent, most infants endure prolonged ileus and cholestasis from parenteral nutrition, and undescended testes in 10 to 20 percent are pushed back without formal orchidopexy at closure.
Large defects accept prosthetic patch with skin cover, and testes left intraabdominal usually descend spontaneously with later orchidopexy only for persistent cases.

Inguinal hernia repair is among the commonest paediatric operations, affecting 3 to 5 percent of term and 9 to 11 percent of premature infants, males sixfold more, right sided in 60 percent, left in 30 percent and bilateral in 10 percent.
Almost all are indirect and congenital from a patent processus vaginalis that should obliterate by the ninth month, giving hernia, communicating hydrocele or cord hydrocele variants.

History and examination diagnose it, the silk glove sign of rubbing peritoneal layers and a thickened cord with intermittent bulge confirm it, and transillumination misleads because thin bowel also lights up.

Incarceration with strangulation risk peaks in the first year and in prematures, so an incarcerated hernia is reduced then repaired in 24 to 48 hours once edema settles, while an irreducible one is a surgical emergency.
Elective premature repair timing is debated with anesthesia neurodevelopment concerns driving trials, and routine repair may wait until apnea risk falls near 1 year of age.
Routine contralateral exploration follows the 4 to 65 percent patent processus rate, and most surgeons explore the other side at or under 2 years of age.
Laparoscopy is increasingly used but meta analysis shows no definite advantage over open repair in children.
Acute hydrocele with epididymitis, torsion or appendage torsion needs ultrasound to separate surgical from medical causes before any hernia decision.
About 80 percent of umbilical hernias close spontaneously, so elective repair waits until around 5 years of age.
Incarceration is extremely rare, separating umbilical hernias from inguinal hernias in urgency.
Earlier repair is considered when the hernia enlarges over time or the fascial defect exceeds 2 cm.
A skin proboscis over 3 cm after neglected closure gives poor cosmesis, which also argues for timely repair.
Repair is always primary fascial closure and prosthetic patch is never used in children.
Observation needs no truss or strapping, and parents are reassured that most defects narrow as the rectus matures.
Defects with incarceration, skin ulceration or evisceration break the elective rule and need prompt surgery.
Umbilical hernias differ from omphalocele by skin cover and small ring, and the two must never be confused in notes or consent.
Pectus excavatum is five times commoner than carinatum, present at birth and worsening to past puberty with a 3 to 4 to 1 male excess from abnormal costal cartilage growth.
Associations include mitral valve prolapse, Ehlers Danlos and Marfan syndromes, so cardiac echo and connective tissue review precede repair.

The Haller index divides chest width by sternovertebral depth on CT or two view films, and repair generally needs two of five criteria including an index above 3.25, restrictive lung disease, cardiac conduction or valve disease, symptoms, or failed prior repair.
The correction index measures regained depth percentage with 28 percent or higher favouring repair, though the cutoff stays controversial.
Best repair age is 10 to 14 years, and the thoracoscopic Nuss bar bent to lift the sternum and flipped convex outward with stabilisers has replaced open Ravitch for most excavatum.
The Nuss bar stays about 2 years while Ravitch bar stays 6 months after cartilage resection and sternal fracture with bundle reattachment.
Enhanced recovery with intercostal cryoablation cuts stay under 2 days, and psychosocial distress over body image in adolescents weighs heavily in the decision.
Carinatum is usually braced with 14 to 16 hours daily wear where adherence predicts success, reserving Ravitch for failures.

modules.name: Hereditary pancreatitis, pancreas divisum and biliary dyskinesia

mustKnow.fact: Hereditary pancreatitis is autosomal dominant with high penetrance from PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen mutation on 7q35, usually R122H or N29I, causing trypsin autoactivation that resists deactivation.
It causes under 1 percent of chronic pancreatitis with bouts from 5 to 10 years without gallstones or divisum, and any child with two unexplained attacks or a family history deserves testing.
Lifetime pancreatic cancer risk rises fifty to seventyfold to 40 percent by age 70, so endoscopic ultrasound screening starts at age 30.
Pancreas divisum is failed ventral and dorsal fusion leaving dorsal Santorini and ventral Wirsung drainage, presenting variably from childhood to adulthood.
Magnetic resonance beats endoscopic retrograde study by showing the whole dorsal duct where retrograde views only the ventral duct, and divisum as a pancreatitis cause stays controversial.
Forced flow through the small minor papilla obstructs and dilates the dorsal duct, treated by transduodenal sphincteroplasty or Puestow pancreaticojejunostomy when dilated or obstructed.
Rising teen obesity brings cholelithiasis and gallbladder dyskinesia into paediatric clinics with classic biliary colic and epigastric pain.
A cholecystokinin HIDA ejection fraction under 35 percent matching colic supports cholecystectomy, while vague noncolicky pain needs another cause first.

Up to 30 percent of preterm infants have an undescended testis against about 2 to 3 percent of full term infants, most descend by 1 year, histologic change starts by 6 months, and Leydig atrophy with impaired spermatogenesis follows by 2 years.

Most arrests are inguinal, retractile testes from a hyperactive cremaster need no surgery, nonpalpable testes may be intraabdominal, absent or vanishing, and ectopic testes lodge in perineum, femoral canal or suprapubic regions.

Palpable inguinal testes get dartos pouch orchidopexy at 6 to 12 months, nonpalpable testes need diagnostic laparoscopy, and intraabdominal testes get two stage Fowler Stephens vessel ligation then orchidopexy 6 months later or single stage laparoscopic mobilisation to the kidney base.
Bilateral nonpalpable testes need human chorionic gonadotropin stimulation testing to prove functioning tissue before laparoscopy hunts for them.
Malignancy risk rises four to fivefold with seminoma commonest, and orchidopexy never lowers the risk but moves the testis where a tumour is found early.
Neonatal extravaginal torsion is an in utero nonsurgical event needing orchiectomy without contralateral fixation, presenting as a firm dark minimally tender hemiscrotum.

Adolescent intravaginal torsion from a bell clapper deformity is a surgical emergency with acute severe pain and a high edematous tender testis, fixed bilaterally after detorsion since the anomaly affects both sides.

Salvage is 90 percent under 6 hours and under 10 percent beyond 24 hours, ultrasound shows absent flow when history and examination leave doubt, radioisotope scanning is most specific, and detorsion goes through a scrotal median raphe approach.
Testicular cancer is under 2 percent of paediatric solid tumours with peaks near 2 years and at puberty, usually found as a painless scrotal mass.
Ultrasound characterises the mass while computed tomography stages retroperitoneal nodes and distant spread.
Alpha fetoprotein from yolk sac marks yolk sac tumours while beta hCG from embryonal carcinoma and mixed teratoma marks choriocarcinoma elements.
Over 95 percent are germ cell tumours split into seminoma and nonseminoma embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma and teratoma, while under 5 percent are Sertoli or Leydig stromal tumours.
Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the operation, nodal or metastatic disease adds systemic chemotherapy with modified retroperitoneal node dissection.
Five year survival is 99.2 percent localised, 96 percent regional and 73 percent distant for germ cell disease.
Stage I non germ cell tumours still cure 80 to 90 percent, but metastatic stromal disease has a median survival of only 1 to 2 years.
Any firm painless paediatric scrotal mass is cancer until proved otherwise, and transscrotal biopsy is avoided in favour of inguinal control.

modules.name: UPJ obstruction, posterior urethral valves and VUR

topics.book: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Ch 576, 577 (Vesicoureteral reflux; Obstruction of the urinary tract)

mustKnow.fact: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is the commonest childhood obstructive lesion from intrinsic stenosis, left sided in 60 percent with a 2 to 1 male excess and bilateral in 10 percent, showing grade 3 or 4 hydronephrosis without a dilated ureter.

Pyeloplasty excising the stenotic segment succeeds in 91 to 98 percent including robotic assisted repair, grade 1 or 2 hydronephrosis with normal parenchyma is watched, and a 3 cm pelvis or poor drainage on MAG3 at 4 to 6 weeks pushes toward surgery.

Posterior urethral valves affect 1 in 8000 males as distal fanning leaflets and are the commonest severe obstructive uropathy, causing bladder hypertrophy, reflux in half and dysplasia by timing and severity with oligohydramnios and lung hypoplasia in severe fetal cases.

Newborn valves present with a palpable walnut bladder and weak stream diagnosed by voiding cystourethrogram, drainage uses a 5 or 8 French feeding tube since a Foley balloon spasms and obstructs, and definitive care is endoscopic valve ablation or temporary vesicostomy when the urethra is too small.

A normal 18 to 24 week scan, creatinine under 0.8 to 1.0 after drainage and visible corticomedullary junction favour the kidney, while oligohydramnios, early hydronephrosis, creatinine above 1.0, bilateral cysts and persistent daytime wetting after 5 years warn of failure, and VURD shunts pressure into one dysplastic kidney to spare the other.

About 30 percent of valve patients reach end stage renal disease and survivors need annual ultrasound, growth, pressure, urine and electrolyte review with lifelong prophylaxis since hydronephrosis persists for years.

Vesicoureteral reflux grades I to V on the maximum voiding cystourethrogram image, low grades usually resolve with a mean resolution age of 6 years while grade V rarely does, and reflux with bladder bowel dysfunction scars kidneys.

The RIVUR trial cut recurrences without cutting scars, prophylaxis targets infants under 1 year and reflux with bladder bowel dysfunction or febrile infection, reimplantation cures 95 to 98 percent of grades I to IV and 80 percent of grade V, and endoscopic bulking cures 70 to 80 percent.
mustKnow.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Ch 576; RIVUR trial

topics.book: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Ch 578, 581 (Anomalies of the bladder; Anomalies of the penis and urethra)

mustKnow.fact: Proximal hypospadias with cryptorchidism demands karyotype and disorder of sex development workup including mixed gonadal dysgenesis, partial androgen insensitivity and congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a virilised female, and 5 to 10 percent of proximal cases carry a dilated prostatic utricle.

The foreskin must never be removed in hypospadias since it supplies repair tissue, ideal repair age is 6 to 12 months, and the tubularised incised plate with vascularised foreskin flap fixes most distal cases in one ambulatory operation.
Complications track severity at 5 percent distal, 10 percent midpenile and 40 percent proximal, led by fistula and meatal stenosis with buccal mucosa graft rescue for complex redos.

Bladder exstrophy occurs in about 1 in 35000 births spanning epispadias to cloacal exstrophy, shows an exposed midline bladder with caudally displaced cord, wide scrotum and dorsal chordee epispadias in males, and leaves total incontinence untreated.
The bladder is covered with plastic wrap never gauze at birth, latex precautions run from nursery to theatre, and transfer goes to a centre with paediatric urology and anaesthesia.

Most undergo bilateral iliac osteotomy to close the pubic symphysis, staged repair closes the bladder first, fixes epispadias at 1 to 2 years and reconstructs the neck at 3 to 6 years once capacity reaches 80 to 90 mL with rectal sphincter control, while single stage repair risks penile injury and hydronephrosis.

Continence reaches 60 to 70 percent in good centres with under 15 percent upper tract deterioration, voiding uses Valsalva or Crede since the neck never relaxes normally, and failures move to augmentation, continent stoma, artificial sphincter or ureterosigmoid diversion.

Ureterosigmoidostomy risks chronic pyelonephritis, chloride and hydrogen absorption acidosis and 15 to 22 percent long term colon cancer, so lifelong surveillance follows any intestinal urinary diversion.
Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest sympathetic tissue, favours abdomen in 65 percent then chest 20 percent with neck and pelvis 5 percent each, and causes 8 to 10 percent of childhood cancers.

Neck tumours compress sympathetic ganglia giving Horner syndrome in 15 percent, spinal extension paralyses rapidly, marrow invasion gives anemia, bruising, bone pain and limping, orbits give raccoon eyes, and skin spread gives blueberry muffin nodules.
Vasoactive intestinal peptide causes intractable diarrhea while cross reactive cerebellar antibodies cause opsoclonus myoclonus with dancing eyes and jerking limbs.

MYCN at 2p24 amplifies in 25 percent overall and 30 to 40 percent of advanced but only 5 percent of localised or 4S disease, 1p36 deletion hits 70 percent of high risk, 11q deletion 15 to 22 percent is unfavourable, and whole chromosome 17 gain is favourable.

Urine catecholamines with vanillylmandelic and homovanillic acids are pathognomonic in infants and toddlers, while lactate dehydrogenase above 1500, ferritin above 142 and neuron specific enolase above 100 support but never prove disease.
Characteristic calcification on cross sectional imaging plus MIBG norepinephrine analogue scanning finds metastases and tracks response, with MRI mapping spinal extension.

Localised disease resects upfront while advanced disease biopsies first for biology then takes induction multidrug chemotherapy before debulking over 90 percent, and image defined risk factors judge resectability after neoadjuvant therapy.

Risk grouping uses age, INSS stage, histology, DNA index and MYCN, stages 1 to 2B resect upfront, advanced disease biopsies first for biology then takes induction chemotherapy before debulking, metastatic disease over 18 months still undergoes delayed primary resection, and 4S infants are watched for spontaneous regression.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 117; COG risk stratification

mustKnow.fact: Wilms tumour is an embryonal metanephric blastema renal neoplasm causing 5.9 percent of paediatric malignancies, 75 percent under 5 years, and bilateral in 13 percent at diagnosis.

WT1 at 11p13 governs kidney, gonad and eye development so mutation brings cryptorchidism, hypospadias and aniridia, WT2 at 11p15 links Beckwith Wiedemann with hemihypertrophy, and WAGR, Denys Drash, Li Fraumeni and neurofibromatosis predispose.

An abdominal mass found by parent or examination leads, with vague pain, hematuria from collecting system invasion, hypertension in 25 percent via renin angiotensin disturbance, and lung metastases in 8 percent.

Ultrasound finds renal vein or caval thrombus, computed tomography separates Wilms from mimics and maps nodes, contralateral kidney and distant spread, and the claw sign with caval thrombus to the atrium is classic.

Favourable histology shows blastemal, stromal and epithelial elements with epithelial predominant behaving gently, while unfavourable means focal or diffuse anaplasia, clear cell sarcoma or rhabdoid tumour with chemoresistance and recurrence.

NWTS stages run I confined and intact, II through capsule or spilled locally, III abdominal residual or nodes, IV hematogenous spread, V bilateral, with caval thrombus upstaging management and any biopsy or spill upstaging the child.

Standard surgery is radical nephrectomy with hilar, paraaortic and paracaval node sampling in en bloc no touch technique, nephron sparing reserved for solitary kidney or bilateral disease after shrinking chemotherapy.

Chemotherapy is vincristine with dactinomycin adding doxorubicin and radiation by stage, favourable stage I reaches near 95 percent survival while unfavourable stages II, III and IV fall to 70, 56 and 17 percent at 4 years.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is an embryonic skeletal muscle cancer causing 4 percent of paediatric malignancy with peaks at 2 to 5 years and 15 to 19 years, enriched in neurofibromatosis type 1 and Li Fraumeni and Beckwith Wiedemann syndromes.

Embryonal including botryoid and spindle forms exceeds two thirds and behaves best, alveolar behaves worst, pleomorphic sits intermediate, and muscle proteins myosin, actin, desmin and myoglobin confirm lineage.

Head and neck leads at 35 percent then genitourinary 25 percent then extremities 20 percent, with orbital proptosis and visual loss, parameningeal headache with bloody nasal discharge, bladder trigone hematuria with obstruction, vaginal grape like botryoid masses, and paratesticular painless scrotal swelling.

No serum marker exists, imaging maps encasement, nodes and metastases, and incisional or core needle biopsy is mandatory since aggressive upfront resection is unnecessary for this chemo and radiosensitive tumour.

Biopsy then risk based chemotherapy is the preferred path, radiation controls microscopic residual and unresectable disease, and vincristine with dactinomycin covers low risk subgroup A with cyclophosphamide added for higher risk.
Clinical grouping runs I fully resected, II grossly resected with microscopic or nodal disease, III gross residual or biopsy only, IV distant metastases at diagnosis.

Three year failure free survival is 88 percent low risk, 55 to 76 percent intermediate and under 30 percent high risk, with 15 percent metastatic at diagnosis and 30 percent relapsing to only 17 percent five year survival.

Extremity lesions need wide local excision with sentinel node mapping and usually radiation for alveolar histology, bladder prostate primaries prioritise organ preservation with preoperative chemoradiation, and paratesticular disease needs radical inguinal orchiectomy with node dissection under 10 years.

Paediatric liver tumours are malignant in 60 percent, hepatoblastoma takes 80 percent of malignant cases and 1 percent of paediatric cancer peaking at 3 years, while hepatocellular carcinoma strikes older children at a median 10 to 11.2 years.

Familial adenomatous polyposis, Gardner and Beckwith Wiedemann raise hepatoblastoma risk, while hepatitis B and C, tyrosinemia, glycogen storage disease type 1, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and biliary atresia cholestasis raise carcinoma risk.
A painless abdominal mass with anorexia, weight loss and anemia leads, jaundice stays rare until late, rupture bleeds into the peritoneum, and a quarter spread to nodes, lung, marrow and brain.

Alpha fetoprotein rises in over 70 percent but also rises in sarcoma, yolk sac tumour and hamartoma under 6 months, all carcinoma suspects need hepatitis testing, and ultrasound plus Doppler map vessels before computed tomography defines anatomy and chest computed tomography hunts lung spread.

PRETEXT divides the liver in four sections by tumour free neighbours from I one involved to IV all involved, adding caudate, rupture, ascites, focality, nodes, metastases and vascular invasion, and stages I and II resect upfront by segmentectomy or lobectomy.

Standard drugs are cisplatin, 5 fluorouracil and vincristine with doxorubicin, irinotecan and ifosfamide for relapse, pure fetal stage I skips chemotherapy, and transplant criteria cap at three tumours under 3 cm without extrahepatic or vascular disease.

Resectable hepatoblastoma exceeds 85 to 90 percent disease free survival matching transplant results for unresectable disease, while carcinoma relapses after partial hepatectomy and earns early transplant consideration.
High risk flags are alpha fetoprotein above 100, spread beyond liver, distant metastases, intraperitoneal bleed and hepatic vein, caval or portal invasion.

Teratomas mix endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm foreign to their site, favour sacrococcygeal, mediastinal, retroperitoneal and gonadal midline sites, run solid cystic or mixed and mature or immature, and affect females in 80 percent with extragonadal disease in neonates and gonadal disease in adolescents.

Sacrococcygeal teratoma takes 60 percent of teratomas, large fetal masses cause polyhydramnios and hydrops with vascular steal high output failure and demise, and raised alpha fetoprotein or beta hCG betrays yolk sac or choriocarcinoma elements.

Prompt resection prevents rupture and bleeding, posterior chevron approach resects tumour with coccyx preserving the anorectum, combined abdominoperineal routes handle intraabdominal extension, and missed coccyx raises recurrence to 37 percent against a 4 to 11 percent baseline.

Diagnosis under 30 weeks gestation or after 2 months postnatal predicts poor outcome, embryonal histology carries 15 to 20 percent malignant transformation, and alpha fetoprotein is tracked every 3 months for 3 to 4 years.

Half of paediatric ovarian lesions are neoplastic but rarely malignant, malignant lesions are 10 percent of masses yet 1 percent of childhood cancers, and germ cell, epithelial and sex cord stromal families divide them.

Malignancy flags are ascites, omental and peritoneal or diaphragmatic implants, adherence, aortoiliac nodes, size above 8 cm and contralateral mass, with teratoma commonest and torsion complicating a quarter, dysgerminoma bilateral in 10 to 15 percent, and granulosa tumours driving precocious puberty.

Surgery spares the ovary for simple cysts and benign teratoma but removes tube and ovary intact for cancer without spill, sampling nodes, washings, implants and contralateral ovary by sight, with bleomycin etoposide cisplatin for spread disease curing 87.5 percent event free and 93.8 percent overall in stage II.
Epithelial tumours stay under 20 percent of paediatric ovarian masses as serous or mucinous adenoma to carcinoma, and androgenic Sertoli Leydig tumours raise testosterone metabolites.

modules.name: Paediatric trauma resuscitation and solid organ injury

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 42 (Management of pediatric trauma)

mustKnow.fact: Blunt injury causes over 90 percent of paediatric trauma, brain injury leads death and disability with 60000 admissions yearly, and children under 4 with hypotension, low Glasgow score, coagulopathy or hypoglycemia fare worst.

Head injury grades mild 13 to 15, moderate 9 to 12 and severe 3 to 8 to communicate severity, while nonaccidental trauma stays on every differential with frenulum tears, subconjunctival bleeding, odd bruises, big head and rib fractures under 3 years carrying 95 percent positive predictive value.

Children desaturate in seconds from high metabolism and low reserve with hypoxia as the top arrest cause, a speaking or crying child proves a patent airway, and a nasogastric tube is banned with basilar skull or midface fracture in favour of an orogastric tube.

Resuscitation gives a 20 mL per kg crystalloid bolus then early O negative blood with massive transfusion thinking, damage control limits crystalloid, balanced transfusion and low titre whole blood gain favour, and tranexamic acid loads 15 mg per kg to 1 g max then 2 mg per kg per hour for 8 hours within 3 hours of injury.

Transfusion doses are red cells 10 to 20 mL per kg, plasma 20 mL per kg, cryoprecipitate 1 unit per 10 kg and platelets 15 mL per kg, with intraosseous access first in the crashing child avoiding injured limbs.

ALARA governs imaging since scanning irradiates growing tissue with dose related brain cancer risk, routine pan scan and stable patient FAST are out, chest computed tomography is selective with thymus mimicking a wide mediastinum, and FAST keeps a role in unstable pericardial and abdominal bleeding.

Liver and spleen lead solid organ injury and grade never dictates care, stable children observe with brief rest and serial haemoglobin, angioembolization is selective by hemodynamics not blush, routine reimaging is out, instability operates, and splenectomy demands encapsulated vaccines plus age based antibiotic prophylaxis against overwhelming sepsis.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 42; APSA solid organ guidelines

mustKnow.fact: Handlebar blows classically injure pancreas and duodenum, low grade pancreatic injury without duct damage observes while distal duct injury gets spleen preserving laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy within 48 hours, duodenal haematoma resolves in 1 to 3 weeks on tube drainage, bowel rest and parenteral nutrition, and perforation operates.
